title: If and when
description: Talk about what happens when, what would happen if, and what you wish.

words.notes: Laiti ningekuwa na… : if only I had…
Also a noun: a rich person.

altBase: When you get there, call me.

altBase: When it rains, we’ll stay home.

altBase: When I get money, I’ll travel.

altBase: If I was rich, I’d buy a car.

dialogues.speaker: juma
dialogues.base: When you get to Mombasa, will you call me?

guidebook.intro: Swahili builds “if” and “when” into the verb: -ki- for real possibilities, -nge- for imagined ones.

phrases.base: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If I were rich, I would buy a car.

tips.title: If and when: -ki-
body: **-ki-** in place of the tense means “if” or “when”: **ukifika** (when you arrive), **nikipata** (if I get), **mvua ikinyesha** (if it rains). The other half of the sentence is usually future or a command: **Ukifika, nipigie.**
You also met it in **Mungu akipenda**, “if God wills”. **Ikiwa** and **kama** also mean “if” as separate words.

tips.title: Would: -nge- on both sides
body: For something imagined, use **-nge-** in both halves: **Ningekuwa tajiri, ningenunua gari** (if I were rich, I would buy a car).
**Laiti** (if only) adds a wish: **Laiti ningekuwa na muda!**

culture.title: Mungu akipenda
body: Plans for tomorrow are often followed by **Mungu akipenda** (if God wills): **Tutaonana kesho, Mungu akipenda.** It’s the -ki- “if” you learned in this unit.

stories.title: If I were rich
stories.summary: Waiting for a matatu, Amani and Juma dream about what they’d do with money.

line.speaker: juma
line.base: Amani, if you were rich, what would you do?

line.speaker: amani
line.base: I would build a school in our village.

line.speaker: juma
line.target: Mimi ningenunua matatu mpya, nzuri kuliko zote!
line.base: I would buy a new matatu, the best of all!

line.speaker: amani
line.target: Na mvua ikinyesha, ningekupa lifti bure?
line.base: And if it rains, would you give me a free lift?

line.speaker: juma
line.base: If you pay the fare, yes!
